title: Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium

questions.topic: Market Price vs. Aggregate Price Indexes
questions.title: Scope of Price (P) in a Single-Product Supply-and-Demand Model
questions.prompt_template: In the microeconomic supply-and-demand model of Chapter 3, what does the vertical-axis variable P represent?

hints.text: Distinguish between analyzing one individual product market and measuring economy-wide inflation.
Think about the units of P in a market like campus iced coffee versus the units of the CPI or GDP Deflator.

options_template.text: The market price of one specific product, measured in dollars per unit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Throughout microeconomic supply-and-demand analysis, P denotes the dollar-per-unit market price of a single product, strictly distinct from economy-wide aggregate price indexes.

options_template.text: An economy-wide aggregate price index such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Micro-Macro Price Conflation): Aggregate price indexes like the CPI measure average prices across a broad basket of goods in Macroeconomics, not a single product's market price.

options_template.text: The GDP Deflator tracking nominal relative to real national output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Aggregate Index Confusion): The GDP Deflator is a macroeconomic price index for total domestic production, not the per-unit price of an individual good.

options_template.text: The total dollar revenue spent across all consumer markets in a year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price vs. Expenditure Confusion): P is a per-unit price, whereas total expenditure equals price multiplied by quantity (P × Q) summed across goods.

questions.topic: Law of Demand and Ceteris Paribus
questions.title: Role of Ceteris Paribus in the Law of Demand
questions.prompt_template: According to the Law of Demand, what relationship holds between a good's own price and its quantity demanded, and why is the ceteris paribus condition essential?

hints.text: Recall the direction in which buyers respond to a higher own price when nothing else changes.
Consider what happens to observed sales if consumer income rises at the exact same time a product's price rises.

options_template.text: They are positively related, and ceteris paribus allows income and tastes to change freely.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Law of Demand): A positive relationship describes the Law of Supply, not the Law of Demand, and ceteris paribus holds non-price factors fixed rather than letting them vary.

options_template.text: They are inversely related, and ceteris paribus holds all non-price determinants constant so the pure price effect is isolated.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Law of Demand states that higher prices reduce quantity demanded (and lower prices raise it) ceteris paribus—holding income, related-good prices, tastes, expectations, and buyer count constant.

options_template.text: They are inversely related, and ceteris paribus holds the product's own price constant while income changes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misapplied Ceteris Paribus): Holding own price constant while changing income describes a demand curve shift, not the movement captured by the Law of Demand.

options_template.text: They are unrelated in the short run unless government price controls are enforced.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero Price Responsiveness Fallacy): Buyers respond to price changes in competitive markets through substitution and purchasing-power effects without needing price controls.

questions.title: Microeconomic Forces Driving the Law of Demand
questions.prompt_template: Which two microeconomic forces explain why a rise in a product's price reduces the quantity demanded by consumers, ceteris paribus?

hints.text: Think about both how consumers compare a more expensive good against rival goods and how the price hike affects their budget.
One force involves switching to relatively cheaper alternatives; the other involves reduced real purchasing power of a fixed paycheck.

options_template.text: The diminishing marginal productivity effect and the fixed-input cost effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Side Attribution): Diminishing marginal productivity and fixed inputs explain rising short-run marginal cost on the seller's side, not consumer demand behavior.

options_template.text: The surplus effect and the market-clearing effect.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Mechanism Confusion): Surpluses and market clearing describe interactions between buyers and sellers across the market, not why an individual demand curve slopes downward.

options_template.text: The substitution effect (alternatives become relatively cheaper) and the income effect (real purchasing power of a fixed paycheck falls).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When a good's price rises, consumers switch toward relatively cheaper alternatives (substitution effect) and can afford less overall with a fixed nominal paycheck (income effect).

options_template.text: The expectations effect (buyers expect higher taxes) and the population effect (fewer buyers enter the market).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve Shifter Confusion): Buyer expectations and the number of buyers are non-price determinants that shift the entire demand curve rather than explaining its downward slope.

questions.topic: Change in Quantity Demanded vs. Change in Demand
questions.title: Distinguishing Own-Price Changes from Demand Shifts
questions.prompt_template: When the price of concert tickets jumps from $60 to $90 and ticket sales decline, which statement accurately describes the market response?

hints.text: Ask whether the event is a change in the product's own price or a change in a non-price determinant.
Remember the rule: never say 'price rose, so demand fell.'

options_template.text: The demand curve for concert tickets shifts leftward because fewer buyers want tickets at $90.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Movement Conflation): A change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve; it moves buyers along the existing curve.

options_template.text: The demand curve shifts rightward to restore ticket revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Driven Shift Fallacy): Higher prices do not cause demand to shift rightward; buyers respond by purchasing a smaller quantity along the stationary curve.

options_template.text: Both the demand curve and the supply curve shift leftward by the same amount.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unwarranted Dual Shift): An own-price change alone causes movement along curves rather than shifting either curve.

options_template.text: Buyers move upward along the existing demand curve to a smaller quantity demanded; the demand curve itself does not shift.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A rise in the ticket's own price from $60 to $90 causes a decrease in quantity demanded (a movement upward along the stationary demand curve), not a shift in demand.

questions.title: Classifying Goods by Their Response to Higher Consumer Income
questions.prompt_template: Suppose household incomes rise across a region, causing demand for fresh produce and airline travel to increase while demand for instant ramen and intercity bus tickets decreases. How are these goods classified?

hints.text: Recall how consumer income shifts demand differently for normal goods versus inferior goods.
Higher income shifts demand rightward for one category and leftward for the other.

options_template.text: Fresh produce and airline travel are normal goods; instant ramen and intercity bus tickets are inferior goods.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By definition, higher consumer income shifts demand rightward for normal goods and leftward for inferior goods.

options_template.text: Fresh produce and airline travel are inferior goods; instant ramen and intercity bus tickets are normal goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normal-Inferior Reversal): This reverses the definitions; normal goods see higher demand when income rises, whereas inferior goods see lower demand.

options_template.text: Fresh produce and instant ramen are complements; airline travel and intercity bus tickets are normal goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Income vs. Cross-Price Confusion): Complements and substitutes are defined by responses to another good's price, not to consumer income.

options_template.text: All four products are substitutes because consumers reallocate their spending across them.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Budget Reallocation Mislabeling): Changing purchases in response to higher income defines normal versus inferior goods, not whether goods are substitutes.

questions.title: Defining Substitutes and Complements via Related-Good Prices
questions.prompt_template: Which pair of statements correctly defines how a price increase in a related good affects demand for a target product?

hints.text: Think of concrete chapter examples: Pepsi and Coca-Cola versus smartphone data plans and smartphones.
When a rival product gets pricier, buyers switch to your product; when a paired product gets pricier, using your product becomes costlier too.

options_template.text: A higher price for a substitute shifts target demand leftward; a higher price for a complement shifts target demand rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Cross-Price Direction): This reverses both effects; pricier substitutes increase target demand, while pricier complements reduce target demand.

options_template.text: A higher price for a substitute shifts target demand rightward; a higher price for a complement shifts target demand leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A price hike for a substitute (such as Pepsi) prompts buyers to switch to the rival good (Coca-Cola), shifting demand rightward; a price hike for a complement (such as smartphone data plans) reduces demand for smartphones, shifting demand leftward.

options_template.text: A higher price for either a substitute or a complement moves buyers along the target good's existing demand curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Own-Price vs. Related-Price Conflation): Only a change in the target good's own price moves buyers along its curve; a change in a related good's price shifts the entire demand curve.

options_template.text: A higher price for a substitute shifts target supply rightward; a higher price for a complement shifts target supply leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Side Confusion): Consumer substitutes and complements are demand determinants, not production-cost determinants of supply.

questions.topic: Buyer Expectations and Number of Buyers
questions.title: How Expectations and Market Size Shift Current Demand
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following events will shift today's market demand curve for a normal good rightward?

hints.text: Review the five non-price demand shifters: income, related-good prices, tastes, expectations, and number of buyers.
Focus on how anticipating higher future prices or experiencing population growth alters buyers' willingness to purchase today.

options_template.text: Buyers expect the product's price to fall sharply next month.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intertemporal Direction Error): Expecting lower future prices encourages buyers to postpone purchases, shifting current demand leftward rather than rightward.

options_template.text: The product's current market price drops by 15%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Movement Conflation): A drop in the good's current own price increases quantity demanded along the existing demand curve without shifting the curve.

options_template.text: Buyers anticipate higher future prices or population growth expands the number of buyers in the market.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expecting higher future prices (or future raises) boosts current demand today, and an increase in the number of buyers shifts market demand outward (rightward).

options_template.text: A technological breakthrough lowers firms' per-unit production costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shifter Misclassification): Cost-reducing technology shifts the supply curve rightward; it is not a non-price determinant of consumer demand.

questions.topic: Law of Supply and Marginal Cost
questions.title: Why Short-Run Supply Curves Typically Slope Upward
questions.prompt_template: According to Chapter 3, what explains the upward slope of a typical short-run supply curve, and what caveat applies to this explanation?

hints.text: Think about the neighborhood bakery running late-afternoon overtime batches with fixed ovens.
Recall whether diminishing marginal productivity is a common short-run explanation or a universal law.

options_template.text: Higher prices lower firms' marginal costs, which is a universal technological law across all industries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Cost Mechanism): Higher market prices do not lower marginal costs; rather, higher prices are needed to cover rising marginal costs of extra units.

options_template.text: Diminishing marginal productivity guarantees that every supply curve in every industry must slope upward in both the short run and the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralization Fallacy): Chapter 3 explicitly cautions that rising marginal cost from diminishing marginal productivity is one common short-run reason for upward-sloping supply, not a universal technological law.

options_template.text: Firms are legally required to expand production proportionally whenever consumer incomes rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal Mandate Misconception): The Law of Supply reflects profit-motivated production decisions comparing market price against marginal cost, not legal mandates.

options_template.text: With some inputs fixed in the short run, diminishing marginal productivity can raise marginal cost (MC) for extra units, so firms supply more only when price covers MC; this is a common reason, not a universal technological law.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When some inputs are fixed in the short run, diminishing marginal productivity can push up marginal cost, requiring higher market prices to justify extra output—though the chapter explicitly notes this is a common reason, not a universal technological law.

questions.title: Distinguishing Supply Shifters from Own-Price Movements
questions.prompt_template: Which combination of changes will unambiguously shift an industry's supply curve rightward?

hints.text: Ask which factors lower marginal production cost or expand total industry capacity at every given price.
Compare input prices, technology, taxes, subsidies, and the number of sellers.

options_template.text: Cost-reducing automation, a government production subsidy, or entry of new firms into the industry.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Process innovations and production subsidies lower marginal cost, and firm entry expands market capacity—all shifting market supply rightward.

options_template.text: An increase in the product's own market price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Movement Conflation): A higher own price increases quantity supplied via a movement upward along the stationary supply curve, not a shift of supply.

options_template.text: Higher raw material prices and a new per-unit business tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Leftward Cost Shifters): Both higher input prices and per-unit taxes raise marginal cost, shifting the supply curve leftward rather than rightward.

options_template.text: Stronger consumer tastes for the product and rising household incomes for a normal good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Shifter Misclassification): Tastes and consumer income are determinants of demand, not non-price determinants of supply.

questions.title: Why Economists Avoid Saying Supply Shifted 'Up' or 'Down'
questions.prompt_template: When rising wages and energy costs raise a bakery's marginal cost per loaf, why is describing the supply change as an 'upward shift' potentially misleading?

hints.text: Check what happens to quantity supplied at any given price when the supply curve moves vertically upward.
Compare the vertical interpretation (higher minimum price) against the horizontal interpretation (smaller quantity at every price).

options_template.text: Because higher input costs always flatten the supply curve into a horizontal line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope vs. Intercept Confusion): A uniform rise in per-unit input cost shifts the supply curve vertically upward (leftward) without turning it horizontal.

options_template.text: Because moving the supply curve vertically upward actually represents a leftward shift—a decrease in quantity supplied at every given price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher input costs mean sellers require a higher minimum price for each unit, which shifts the supply curve vertically upward—equivalently, leftward to a smaller quantity supplied at every price.

options_template.text: Because an upward vertical move on a supply graph means firms are willing to supply more output at every price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Up-Equals-Increase Fallacy): Confusing 'up' with 'more' is the exact error Chapter 3 warns against; a vertically higher supply curve sits to the left and supplies less at every price.

options_template.text: Because supply curves can only shift horizontally and never change their vertical price intercept.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Geometry Misconception): For any positively sloped linear supply curve, a leftward shift simultaneously raises the vertical intercept (minimum supply price).

questions.title: Purpose of the Nonnegativity Restriction in Linear Supply
questions.prompt_template: In the linear supply model Q_s = d(P - P_min) for P >= P_min, why does Chapter 3 explicitly set Q_s = 0 for all prices below P_min?

hints.text: Plug a price smaller than P_min into the algebraic formula d(P - P_min) and inspect the sign of the result.
Consider whether a firm can physically supply a negative number of loaves of bread or generators.

options_template.text: To ensure the supply curve becomes downward-sloping at low prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Inversion Error): Setting Q_s = 0 below P_min places the supply curve along the vertical axis rather than giving it a negative slope.

options_template.text: Because P_min represents the choke price where consumers stop buying the product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Choke Price vs. Minimum Supply Price Confusion): The choke price is the demand curve's vertical intercept where Q_d = 0; P_min is the supply curve's vertical intercept where Q_s = 0.

options_template.text: To avoid interpreting a negative algebraic value of Q_s as actual market supply when market price falls below sellers' minimum acceptable price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Below P_min, the linear expression d(P - P_min) becomes negative, so the piecewise model sets Q_s = 0 to prevent interpreting negative numbers as actual physical supply.

options_template.text: Because firms must always earn zero profit when market price exceeds P_min.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Profit vs. Supply Intercept Confusion): P_min is the threshold price below which firms offer zero units; it does not imply zero profit at higher prices.

questions.title: Price Adjustment Pressures in Surplus vs. Shortage
questions.prompt_template: How do market forces respond when a product's current price differs from the equilibrium price P*?

hints.text: Compare quantity demanded and quantity supplied above P* versus below P*.
Ask whether unsold inventories push prices down or unmet buyer demand bids prices up.

options_template.text: At any price above P*, a shortage occurs and buyers bid prices upward; at any price below P*, a surplus occurs and sellers cut prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): Prices above P* generate excess supply (surplus), not a shortage, and prices below P* generate excess demand (shortage), not a surplus.

options_template.text: Market equilibrium occurs whenever total quantity supplied is greater than or equal to total quantity demanded.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-as-Equilibrium Fallacy): If Q_s strictly exceeds Q_d, there is a surplus and downward pressure on price; equilibrium requires exact equality Q_d = Q_s.

options_template.text: At any price above P*, the demand curve automatically shifts rightward until the surplus disappears.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disequilibrium Shift Fallacy): Market adjustment from a non-equilibrium price occurs via price changes moving buyers and sellers along their existing curves, not by shifting curves.

options_template.text: At any price above P*, a surplus (excess supply) pressures sellers to cut prices; at any price below P*, a shortage (excess demand) bids prices upward toward P*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When P > P*, Q_s > Q_d (surplus), pressuring sellers to lower prices; when P < P*, Q_d > Q_s (shortage), bidding prices upward until Q_d = Q_s at P*.

questions.title: When an Equilibrium Outcome Becomes Ambiguous
questions.prompt_template: Under the three-step comparative statics protocol, why does one equilibrium variable (either P* or Q*) become ambiguous when demand and supply shift simultaneously?

hints.text: Trace the separate effect of each curve shift on P* and on Q*.
When two simultaneous shifts push the same variable in opposite directions, what extra information is needed to sign the net change?

options_template.text: Because one variable is pushed in the same direction by both shifts while the other is pushed in opposite directions, so its net change depends on which shift is larger.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Whenever both curves shift, one variable moves unambiguously because both shifts reinforce it, while the other is pulled in opposite directions and cannot be signed without knowing relative shift magnitudes.

options_template.text: Because simultaneous shifts violate the Law of Demand and make both curves vertical.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law Violation Fallacy): Simultaneous shifts preserve both the Law of Demand and the Law of Supply; ambiguity comes from opposing directional effects.

options_template.text: Because comparative statics can only analyze one market event per calendar year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Artificial Method Limit): Comparative statics handles simultaneous shifts routinely by combining the directional predictions of each shift.

options_template.text: Because whenever both curves shift at once, both P* and Q* always remain completely unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exact Cancellation Fallacy): Exact cancellation is a knife-edge coincidence for the opposing variable, and the reinforced variable must strictly rise or fall.

questions.title: Interpreting Points A, B, and C on a Demand Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In a demand diagram (like Figure 1 in Chapter 3), point A is (Q=10, P=$80) and point B is (Q=20, P=$60) on curve D1, while point C is (Q=30, P=$60) on curve D2. What do the transitions A -> B and B -> C represent?

hints.text: Check whether price changes between A and B, and whether price changes between B and C.
A move along one curve at two different prices is a change in quantity demanded; a horizontal move at the same price to a new curve is a change in demand.

options_template.text: A -> B is an increase in demand; B -> C is an increase in quantity demanded.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement-Shift Label Swap): Between A and B, own price drops from $80 to $60 along D1 (quantity demanded); between B and C, price stays at $60 while the curve shifts to D2 (demand).

options_template.text: A -> B is a movement along D1 (increase in quantity demanded due to a price drop from $80 to $60); B -> C is a rightward shift of demand (increase in demand at $60 caused by a non-price factor).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lowering own price from $80 to $60 moves buyers along D1 from A to B; a non-price factor such as higher income shifts the entire curve from D1 to D2, raising quantity demanded at $60 from 20 to 30.

options_template.text: Both A -> B and B -> C represent rightward shifts of the demand curve caused by lower prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Causes-Shift Fallacy): Own-price changes never shift the demand curve; only B -> C is a curve shift, and it is driven by a non-price determinant.

options_template.text: A -> B represents a surplus of 10 units; B -> C represents a shortage of 10 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Curve Disequilibrium Confusion): Surpluses and shortages require comparing both a demand curve and a supply curve at the same price; Figure 1 shows only demand curves.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Rival Soft Drink Price Hike
questions.prompt_template: Pepsi and Coca-Cola are substitutes. If the price of Pepsi increases sharply, how is this change depicted on the supply-and-demand graph for Coca-Cola?

hints.text: Ask whether the price of Pepsi is the own price on the vertical axis of the Coca-Cola market graph.
When Pepsi becomes more expensive, consumers want more Coca-Cola at every Coca-Cola price.

options_template.text: A movement upward along the existing demand curve for Coca-Cola.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Own-Price Conflation): Pepsi's price is not on the vertical axis of the Coca-Cola graph; changing a substitute's price shifts the Coca-Cola demand curve.

options_template.text: A leftward shift of the demand curve for Coca-Cola, lowering both P* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Substitute-Complement Confusion): A leftward shift occurs when the price of a complement rises, not when the price of a substitute rises.

options_template.text: A rightward shift of the demand curve for Coca-Cola, raising both equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A higher price for the substitute (Pepsi) shifts the demand curve for Coca-Cola rightward, leading to a higher equilibrium price and higher equilibrium quantity of Coca-Cola.

options_template.text: A rightward shift of the supply curve for Coca-Cola, lowering P* and raising Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Side Confusion): Consumer substitution between Pepsi and Coca-Cola changes buyer demand, not Coca-Cola's production costs or supply curve.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of Higher Smartphone Data-Plan Prices
questions.prompt_template: Smartphones and smartphone data plans are complements. If wireless carriers substantially raise the price of smartphone data plans, what happens on the market diagram for smartphones?

hints.text: Consider how pricier data plans change buyers' willingness to purchase a smartphone at any given smartphone price.
Determine which curve shifts and in which direction, then read the new intersection with an unchanged supply curve.

options_template.text: Buyers move downward along the existing demand curve for smartphones without shifting either curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Own-Price Conflation): The price that changed is for data plans, not smartphones, so the smartphone demand curve must shift.

options_template.text: The demand curve for smartphones shifts rightward, raising both P* and Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Complement-Substitute Reversal): Buyers do not buy more smartphones when data plans get more expensive; that rightward shift would describe substitutes.

options_template.text: The supply curve for smartphones shifts leftward, raising P* and lowering Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Input vs. Complement Confusion): Consumer data plans are a complementary good purchased by buyers, not a manufacturing input paid by smartphone factories.

options_template.text: The demand curve for smartphones shifts leftward, reducing both equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because data plans are complements to smartphones, higher data-plan prices reduce demand for smartphones (leftward shift), lowering both P* and Q*.

questions.topic: Income Shift for an Inferior Good
questions.title: Graphical Response of Instant Ramen to Rising Household Incomes
questions.prompt_template: Instant ramen is an inferior good. If average household incomes rise significantly across an economy while ramen production costs are unchanged, what happens in the instant ramen market?

hints.text: First identify whether higher income shifts demand right or left for an inferior good.
Then trace the new intersection along the upward-sloping supply curve to determine P* and Q*.

options_template.text: Demand shifts leftward; equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity falls.
options_template.feedback: Correct. For an inferior good, rising consumer income shifts the demand curve leftward, reducing both equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*.

options_template.text: Demand shifts rightward; equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Normal-Good Default Fallacy): Treating every good as normal overlooks that higher income lowers demand for inferior goods like instant ramen.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward; equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Supply Side Confusion): Consumer income is a demand shifter, not a supply shifter, and ramen production costs were explicitly held constant.

options_template.text: Supply shifts rightward; equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Curve Shifted): Higher consumer income alters household demand for ramen rather than lowering manufacturers' marginal costs.

questions.title: Reading a Cost-Reducing Technological Shift on a Supply Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In a supply diagram (like Figure 2 in Chapter 3), cost-reducing technology shifts supply from S1 to S2 so that at P = $60, quantity supplied expands from 20 units to 25 units. How does S2 sit visually relative to S1?

hints.text: Check both the horizontal direction (at a fixed price of $60) and the vertical direction (at a fixed quantity of 20).
Lower marginal cost means sellers supply more at $60 and require a lower minimum price for any given quantity.

options_template.text: S2 lies to the left of (and vertically above) S1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Left-Right Inversion): A curve lying to the left and above S1 indicates higher marginal costs and smaller quantity supplied at $60.

options_template.text: S2 lies to the right of (and vertically below) S1.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A cost-reducing technological improvement shifts supply rightward (vertically downward), meaning firms offer more units at $60 (25 instead of 20) and accept a lower price for every quantity.

options_template.text: S2 is identical to S1, and the move from 20 to 25 units is a movement along S1.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Movement Conflation): Price stayed constant at $60 while quantity supplied rose from 20 to 25; moving along a fixed curve requires price to change.

options_template.text: S2 rotates to become downward-sloping because marginal costs become negative.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Slope Fallacy): Lowering marginal cost shifts an upward-sloping supply curve rightward/downward; it does not make marginal cost negative or flip the curve's slope.

questions.topic: Per-Unit Business Tax vs. Production Subsidy
questions.title: Comparing Supply-Curve Shifts from Taxes and Subsidies
questions.prompt_template: How do a new per-unit business tax and a government production subsidy affect a market's supply curve and equilibrium, assuming standard downward-sloping demand?

hints.text: Determine how each policy alters a seller's marginal cost per unit produced.
Remember: higher marginal cost shifts supply leftward; lower marginal cost shifts supply rightward.

options_template.text: A per-unit tax shifts supply rightward (lowering P*, raising Q*); a subsidy shifts supply leftward (raising P*, lowering Q*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Subsidy Reversal): A tax adds to per-unit cost and shrinks supply, whereas a subsidy offsets cost and expands supply.

options_template.text: Both a per-unit tax and a production subsidy shift supply rightward because both involve government intervention.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intervention Uniformity Fallacy): Taxes and subsidies act in opposite directions on firms' marginal costs and therefore shift supply in opposite directions.

options_template.text: A per-unit tax shifts supply leftward (raising P*, lowering Q*); a production subsidy shifts supply rightward (lowering P*, raising Q*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A per-unit business tax raises marginal cost, shifting supply leftward (higher P*, lower Q*), whereas a production subsidy lowers marginal cost, shifting supply rightward (lower P*, higher Q*).

options_template.text: Neither policy shifts supply; both cause movements along the existing supply curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-as-Movement Fallacy): Per-unit taxes and subsidies alter sellers' net marginal cost at every price, shifting the entire supply curve.

questions.title: Identifying Disequilibrium Above Equilibrium Price
questions.prompt_template: In a market diagram (like Figure 3 in Chapter 3), original equilibrium is E1*(Q=20, P=$60). At a horizontal price line of P = $80, the line intersects D1 at Q = 10 and S at Q = 30. What does the horizontal segment between Q = 10 and Q = 30 represent?

hints.text: Compare quantity supplied against quantity demanded at P = $80.
The horizontal distance Q_s - Q_d at a price above equilibrium measures excess supply.

options_template.text: A shortage of 20 units, creating upward pressure on price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): At $80, Q_s (30) exceeds Q_d (10), which is excess supply (surplus), not a shortage.

options_template.text: A new market equilibrium with 30 units sold at $80.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Supplied-as-Sales Fallacy): At $80, buyers only purchase 10 units, leaving 20 unsold; the market does not clear at $80.

options_template.text: A rightward shift of the supply curve by 20 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Disequilibrium-as-Shift Fallacy): The 20-unit gap is a disequilibrium gap between two stationary curves at $80, not a shift of the supply curve.

options_template.text: A surplus of 20 units, creating downward pressure on price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = $80, sellers offer 30 units while buyers want only 10 units, creating a surplus of 30 - 10 = 20 units that pressures sellers to cut prices toward $60.

questions.topic: Adjustment Process After a Demand Shift
questions.title: How Price Adjusts Between Old and New Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: In Figure 3 of Chapter 3, equilibrium starts at E1*(Q=20, P=$60). Demand shifts rightward from D1 to D2, and the new equilibrium is E2*(Q=25, P=$70). What disequilibrium immediately occurs at the old price of $60, and how does supply respond during the transition?

hints.text: Hold price momentarily at $60 right after D1 shifts to D2 and compare Q_d on D2 with Q_s on S.
Does the supply curve itself shift, or do sellers move upward along the stationary supply curve as price rises from $60 to $70?

options_template.text: A shortage occurs at $60, bidding price upward to $70 and causing an upward movement along the stationary supply curve S (higher quantity supplied from 20 to 25).
options_template.feedback: Correct. At $60, D2 exceeds S, creating a temporary shortage that bids price up to $70; higher price induces sellers to move upward along the existing supply curve from 20 to 25 units.

options_template.text: A surplus occurs at $60, causing the supply curve to shift leftward until P reaches $70.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Disequilibrium & Unwarranted Supply Shift): A rightward demand shift creates a shortage (not surplus) at the old price, and the supply curve does not shift.

options_template.text: A shortage occurs at $60, causing the supply curve to shift rightward to meet D2 at Q = 25.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply Shift vs. Quantity Supplied Confusion): Higher price caused by a demand shift increases quantity supplied along S; it does not shift the supply curve.

options_template.text: No disequilibrium occurs because price jumps instantaneously without any excess demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Price-Adjustment Mechanism): In comparative statics, the temporary excess demand (shortage) at the old price is precisely the economic force that drives price upward.

questions.title: Campus Coffee Shop Facing a New Rival Café
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a popular new café opens directly across the street from the campus coffee shop, while the original shop's bean and labor costs do not change. According to Table 1 (Comparative Statics), how do equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q* change at the original shop?

hints.text: A rival café is a substitute option that draws away customers from the original shop.
Shift demand leftward along a stationary upward-sloping supply curve and inspect the new intersection.

options_template.text: Demand shifts leftward; P* rises and Q* falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Leftward Supply Outcome Applied to Demand): Rising P* with falling Q* is the signature of a leftward supply shift, not a leftward demand shift.

options_template.text: Demand shifts leftward; P* falls and Q* falls.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Competition from a nearby substitute shifts demand for the original shop leftward, reducing both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward; P* rises and Q* falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Curve-Side Confusion): A rival café taking away buyers alters demand for the original shop, not its marginal production costs.

options_template.text: Demand shifts rightward; P* rises and Q* rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Losing customers to a new competitor decreases demand (leftward shift), not increases it.

questions.title: Impact of a Spike in Roasted Coffee-Bean Costs
questions.prompt_template: Suppose roasted coffee-bean costs jump sharply while student demand for campus iced lattes remains unchanged. Which graphical shift and equilibrium outcome follow?

hints.text: Roasted coffee beans are a key production input for lattes.
Higher input costs shift supply leftward (vertically upward) along a stationary downward-sloping demand curve.

options_template.text: Supply shifts rightward; P* falls and Q* rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Direction Reversal): Higher input costs raise marginal cost and reduce supply (leftward), rather than expanding it.

options_template.text: Demand shifts leftward; P* falls and Q* falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Input-Cost-as-Demand-Shifter): Input costs affect sellers' supply curve; buyers' demand curve does not shift when bean costs rise.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward; P* rises and Q* falls.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher coffee-bean costs shift the supply curve leftward, moving the market equilibrium upward along the demand curve to a higher P* and lower Q*.

options_template.text: Supply shifts leftward; P* rises and Q* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Shift Ambiguity Error): Ambiguity only arises when both curves shift simultaneously; a single leftward supply shift unambiguously raises P* and lowers Q*.

questions.topic: Simultaneous Shifts: Both D and S Increase
questions.title: AI Server Demand Boom and New Semiconductor Fab Capacity
questions.prompt_template: Suppose surging demand for AI servers shifts semiconductor demand rightward at the same time new fabrication capacity shifts semiconductor supply rightward. Under standard downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply, what happens to P* and Q*?

hints.text: List the separate effect of D rightward (P up, Q up) and S rightward (P down, Q up).
Combine the two effects: which variable is pushed in the same direction, and which is pushed in opposite directions?

options_template.text: Both P* and Q* unambiguously rise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Supply Price Effect): While demand growth pushes price up, expanded supply pushes price down, making the net change in P* ambiguous.

options_template.text: P* unambiguously rises, while Q* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Ambiguity): Both rightward shifts expand Q*, so Q* is unambiguous while P* is ambiguous.

options_template.text: P* unambiguously falls, while Q* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dominant-Supply Assumption): Assuming P* falls implicitly assumes the supply shift is larger than the demand shift, which is not given.

options_template.text: Q* unambiguously rises, while the net change in P* is ambiguous without knowing the relative sizes of the shifts.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both a rightward demand shift and a rightward supply shift raise equilibrium quantity Q*, whereas their opposing effects on price make P* ambiguous.

questions.topic: Simultaneous Shifts: D Increases and S Decreases
questions.title: Finals Week Demand Surge Combined with Higher Bean Costs
questions.prompt_template: During finals week, student demand for campus coffee shifts rightward at the exact same time higher roasted coffee-bean costs shift supply leftward. What does Table 1 (Comparative Statics) predict for P* and Q*?

hints.text: Write out D right (P up, Q up) and S left (P up, Q down).
Identify which variable is reinforced by both shifts and which variable faces opposing pressures.

options_template.text: P* unambiguously rises, while the net change in Q* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both higher demand and lower supply push equilibrium price upward, while higher demand raises Q* and lower supply reduces Q*, leaving Q* ambiguous.

options_template.text: Q* unambiguously rises, while P* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Simultaneous-Shift Case): That outcome applies when both D and S shift rightward, not when D increases and S decreases.

options_template.text: P* unambiguously rises and Q* unambiguously falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Demand Quantity Effect): Although lower supply pushes Q* down, higher demand pushes Q* up, so Q* cannot be signed without shift magnitudes.

options_template.text: Both P* and Q* are ambiguous whenever curves shift in opposite directions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Ambiguity Fallacy): In every two-curve simultaneous shift case, one variable is always unambiguous; here both shifts push P* upward.

questions.topic: Simultaneous Shifts: D Decreases vs. S Shifts
questions.title: Comparing (D Left, S Right) Against (D Left, S Left)
questions.prompt_template: How do the comparative statics predictions differ between Case 1 (demand decreases and supply increases) and Case 2 (both demand and supply decrease)?

hints.text: Evaluate P* and Q* separately for each case using Table 1.
Check which variable is reinforced when D goes left and S goes right (price falls from both) versus when both go left (quantity falls from both).

options_template.text: In Case 1, Q* falls and P* is ambiguous; in Case 2, P* falls and Q* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Case-Swap Error): This swaps the two cases; Case 1 unambiguously lowers P* while Case 2 unambiguously lowers Q*.

options_template.text: In Case 1, P* unambiguously falls and Q* is ambiguous; in Case 2, Q* unambiguously falls and P* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When D decreases and S increases, both shifts push P* downward while opposing each other on Q*. When both D and S decrease, both shifts push Q* downward while opposing each other on P*.

options_template.text: In both Case 1 and Case 2, P* unambiguously falls and Q* unambiguously falls.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Opposing Effects): Simultaneous shifts always create opposing pressures on one variable, leaving it ambiguous without relative shift magnitudes.

options_template.text: In Case 1, P* rises and Q* is ambiguous; in Case 2, Q* rises and P* is ambiguous.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Lower demand and higher supply both reduce P* (not raise it), and lower demand plus lower supply both reduce Q* (not raise it).

questions.title: Inverting a Linear Demand Function and Finding the Choke Price
questions.prompt_template: Monthly demand for a campus streaming bundle is given by Q_d = 360 - 8P, where P is the monthly price in dollars. What are the inverse demand equation and the choke price?

hints.text: Solve Q_d = 360 - 8P for P by isolating 8P on one side and dividing every term by 8.
The choke price is the vertical intercept where Q_d = 0.

options_template.text: P = 45 - 8Q_d, with a choke price of $45.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uninverted Slope Error): Dividing 360 by 8 correctly gives 45, but you must also divide the Q_d coefficient by 8 to obtain -0.125Q_d rather than -8Q_d.

options_template.text: P = 360 - 0.125Q_d, with a choke price of $360.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Undivided Intercept Error): You must divide both 360 and Q_d by 8 when isolating P; 360 is the horizontal quantity intercept, not the choke price.

options_template.text: P = 45 - 0.125Q_d, with a choke price of $45.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Solving 8P = 360 - Q_d gives P = 45 - 0.125Q_d; setting Q_d = 0 yields the choke price P_choke = $45.

options_template.text: P = 45 + 0.125Q_d, with a choke price of $45.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Flip Error): Because demand obeys the Law of Demand, inverse demand must have a negative slope (-0.125), not a positive slope.

questions.title: Evaluating Quantity Demanded After a Rightward Demand Shift
questions.prompt_template: Original monthly demand for campus cold-brew passes is Q_d = 500 - 10P. During exam month, student demand increases by 75 passes at every price level. What is the new quantity demanded at P = $20?

hints.text: First write the shifted demand equation by adding 75 to the horizontal intercept (500), or evaluate original Q_d at $20 and then add 75.

options_template.text: 300 passes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Demand Shift): 500 - 10(20) = 300 is the original quantity demanded before the +75-unit rightward shift.

options_template.text: 225 passes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Shift Sign): 300 - 75 = 225 subtracts the shift instead of adding an increase in demand.

options_template.text: 575 passes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-as-Quantity Error): 575 is the new horizontal intercept at P = $0; it omits subtracting 10P = 200.

options_template.text: 375 passes.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The shifted equation is Q_d_new = 575 - 10P; at P = $20, Q_d_new = 575 - 10(20) = 375 passes (equivalently, original 300 + 75 = 375).

questions.topic: Inverse Supply and Minimum Supply Price
questions.title: Inverting a Linear Supply Function to Find P_min
questions.prompt_template: Local coffee roasters supply bags of beans according to Q_s = -60 + 10P (for P >= $6). What are the inverse supply equation and the minimum supply price P_min?

hints.text: Add 60 to both sides to get 10P = 60 + Q_s, then divide every term by 10.
Set Q_s = 0 in the inverse supply equation to read off P_min.

options_template.text: P = 6 + 0.1Q_s, with P_min = $6.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Solving 10P = 60 + Q_s gives P = 6 + 0.1Q_s; at Q_s = 0, the minimum supply price is P_min = $6.

options_template.text: P = -6 + 0.1Q_s, with P_min = -$6.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error Moving -60): Moving -60 across the equals sign changes its sign to +60, yielding a positive minimum supply price of +$6.

options_template.text: P = 6 + 10Q_s, with P_min = $6.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uninverted Slope Error): Dividing by 10 converts the Q_s coefficient to 1/10 = 0.1, not 10.

options_template.text: P = 60 + 0.1Q_s, with P_min = $60.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Undivided Intercept Error): You must divide 60 by 10 when solving for P; 60/10 = $6, not $60.

questions.title: Computing Shifted Quantity Supplied After a Per-Unit Cost Increase
questions.prompt_template: Neighborhood bakeries supply artisan loaves according to Q_s = -40 + 8P for P >= $5 (inverse supply P = 5 + 0.125Q_s). Higher flour and electricity prices raise sellers' minimum acceptable price by $4 per loaf at every quantity. At P = $14, how many loaves are supplied under the new supply curve?

hints.text: Add $4 to the vertical intercept of the inverse supply equation to get P_new = 9 + 0.125Q_s.
Invert back to direct form Q_s_new = 8(P - 9) = -72 + 8P, then substitute P = $14.

options_template.text: 72 loaves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Cost Shift): -40 + 8(14) = 72 uses the original pre-shift supply curve.

options_template.text: 40 loaves.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding $4 to the inverse supply intercept gives P_new = 9 + 0.125Q_s, or Q_s_new = -72 + 8P for P >= $9. At P = $14, Q_s_new = -72 + 8(14) = 40 loaves.

options_template.text: 68 loaves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-vs.-Quantity Shift Confusion): Subtracting 4 directly from quantity (-44 + 8(14) = 68) ignores that a $4 vertical price shift reduces quantity supplied by 8 × 4 = 32 loaves.

options_template.text: 76 loaves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Direction and Axis Error): Adding 4 directly to quantity (-36 + 8(14) = 76) both treats a cost hike as a supply increase and applies a dollar shift to quantity.

questions.title: Applying the Nonnegativity Restriction Below P_min
questions.prompt_template: A market's initial supply is Q_s = -50 + 5P for P >= $10 (with P_min = $10). A new $5 per-unit business tax raises sellers' minimum acceptable price to $15, yielding Q_s_new = -75 + 5P for P >= $15 and Q_s_new = 0 for P < $15. What is the quantity supplied under the new curve at P = $12?

hints.text: Compare the given market price ($12) against the new minimum supply price ($15) before substituting into the linear formula.
Recall the piecewise supply definition for prices strictly below P_min.

options_template.text: -15 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unrestricted Negative Quantity): Plugging P = $12 blindly into -75 + 5(12) yields -15, violating the nonnegativity restriction because firms cannot supply negative physical units.

options_template.text: 10 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored Tax Shift): -50 + 5(12) = 10 evaluates the pre-tax supply curve instead of the post-tax schedule.

options_template.text: 0 units.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $12 is below the new minimum supply price of $15, sellers are unwilling to produce any units, so the piecewise supply function sets Q_s_new = 0.

options_template.text: 5 units.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Axis Tax Error): Subtracting 5 directly from the quantity equation (-55 + 5(12) = 5) misapplies a $5 per-unit price shift to the quantity axis.

questions.title: Solving for Equilibrium Price and Quantity from Direct Equations
questions.prompt_template: In a regional market for electric bike helmets, demand is Q_d = 600 - 3P and supply is Q_s = -120 + 5P (for P >= $24). What are the market equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q*?

hints.text: Set Q_d = Q_s so that 600 - 3P = -120 + 5P, collect constants on one side and P terms on the other.
Once you find P*, substitute it into both Q_d and Q_s to verify they yield the exact same Q*.

options_template.text: P* = $60, Q* = 420 helmets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant Sign Error): Subtracting 120 from 600 instead of adding gives 480 = 8P -> P = $60, where Q_d = 420 but Q_s = 180 (not equilibrium).

options_template.text: P* = $120, Q* = 240 helmets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Addition Error): Dividing 720 by 6 instead of 8 (= 5 + 3) yields P = $120, where Q_d = 240 and Q_s = 480.

options_template.text: P* = $90, Q* = 270 helmets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incomplete Substitution Error): P* = $90 is correct, but 3(90) = 270 is only the subtracted term—you must compute 600 - 270 = 330.

options_template.text: P* = $90, Q* = 330 helmets.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 600 - 3P = -120 + 5P gives 720 = 8P, so P* = $90. Substituting into either equation yields Q* = 600 - 3(90) = 330 (check: -120 + 5(90) = 330).

questions.title: Solving for Equilibrium from Inverse Demand and Inverse Supply
questions.prompt_template: A market has inverse demand P = 140 - 2Q and inverse supply P = 20 + 4Q. What are the equilibrium quantity Q* and equilibrium price P*?

hints.text: Set the two price expressions equal: 140 - 2Q = 20 + 4Q, and solve for Q* first.
Substitute Q* back into either inverse equation to find P*, and double-check that you do not swap Q* and P*.

options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 140 - 2Q = 20 + 4Q gives 120 = 6Q, so Q* = 20 units. Plugging Q* = 20 into either equation gives P* = 140 - 2(20) = $100 (check: 20 + 4(20) = $100).
Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped P* and Q* Coordinates): The numerical values 20 and 100 are correct, but Q* = 20 units and P* = $100, not the reverse.
Diagnostic fallacy (Subtracted Slopes Error): Computing 4Q - 2Q = 2Q instead of 4Q + 2Q = 6Q gives 2Q = 120 -> Q = 60, where inverse supply would be $260, not $20.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Demand Slope): Setting 4Q = 120 omits adding the 2Q term from the demand side; at Q = 30, P_d = $80 while P_s = $140.

questions.title: Measuring Excess Supply Above Market Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: In a city's market for portable solar generators, demand is Q_d = 500 - 2P and supply is Q_s = -100 + 4P (for P >= $25), so equilibrium is P* = $100 and Q* = 300. If the market price is $130, what disequilibrium occurs and what is its exact size?

hints.text: Evaluate both Q_d(130) and Q_s(130) separately.
Compare Q_s and Q_d to classify surplus vs. shortage, then take the difference |Q_s - Q_d|.

options_template.text: A shortage of 180 generators.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): At $130 (above P* = $100), Q_s = 420 exceeds Q_d = 240, so the 180-unit gap is a surplus, not a shortage.

options_template.text: A surplus of 180 generators.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = $130, Q_d = 500 - 2(130) = 240 and Q_s = -100 + 4(130) = 420. Because Q_s > Q_d, there is a surplus of 420 - 240 = 180 generators.

options_template.text: A surplus of 60 generators.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Gap-Only Error): 300 - 240 = 60 measures only the drop in Q_d below Q*, ignoring the simultaneous rise in Q_s to 420.

options_template.text: A surplus of 120 generators.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium-Baseline Error): 420 - 300 = 120 subtracts the equilibrium quantity Q* instead of the actual quantity demanded Q_d(130) = 240.

questions.title: Measuring Excess Demand Below Market Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Demand for campus commuter bike lockers is Q_d = 480 - 4P and supply is Q_s = -60 + 2P (for P >= $30), with equilibrium P* = $90 and Q* = 120. If the rental price is set at P = $70, what disequilibrium results?

hints.text: Substitute P = $70 into both Q_d and Q_s.
Because $70 is below P* = $90, verify Q_d > Q_s and compute Q_d - Q_s.

options_template.text: A shortage of 80 lockers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium-Baseline Error): 200 - 120 = 80 compares Q_d(70) against Q* = 120 instead of against Q_s(70) = 80.

options_template.text: A surplus of 120 lockers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shortage-Surplus Inversion): At $70, buyers want 200 lockers while only 80 are supplied, creating excess demand (a shortage), not a surplus.

options_template.text: A shortage of 120 lockers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = $70, Q_d = 480 - 4(70) = 200 and Q_s = -60 + 2(70) = 80. Because Q_d > Q_s, there is a shortage of 200 - 80 = 120 lockers.

options_template.text: A shortage of 40 lockers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Gap-Only Error): 120 - 80 = 40 measures only the fall in Q_s below Q*, ignoring that Q_d also rose to 200.

questions.title: Finding the New Equilibrium After a Rightward Demand Shift
questions.prompt_template: A market initially has demand Q_d = 420 - 2P and supply Q_s = -60 + 4P (for P >= $15), giving initial equilibrium P1* = $80 and Q1* = 260. Higher consumer income then increases demand by 90 units at every price (Q_d_new = 510 - 2P). What is the new equilibrium (P2*, Q2*)?

hints.text: Set the new demand equation equal to the unchanged supply equation: 510 - 2P = -60 + 4P.
Solve for P2*, then plug P2* into Q_d_new or Q_s to find Q2* (note that Q2* will rise by less than 90 because rising price moderates quantity demanded).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Shift Error): Assuming P* stays at $80 and adding all 90 units to Q1* = 260 ignores the shortage at $80 that bids price upward.

Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Shift Quantity Error): Although P2* = $95 is right, adding the full 90-unit horizontal shift to Q1* = 260 ignores that the $15 price increase moves buyers upward along D2 by 30 units (350 - 30 = 320).
Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Shift Direction): Subtracting 90 instead of adding 90 gives Q_d_new = 330 - 2P, yielding P = $65 and Q = 200.

questions.title: Finding the New Equilibrium After a Rightward Supply Shift
questions.prompt_template: Initial market demand is Q_d = 600 - 4P and initial supply is Q_s = -120 + 6P (for P >= $20), giving P1* = $72 and Q1* = 312. A technological improvement shifts supply rightward by 120 units at every price, so Q_s_new = 6P (for P >= $0). What is the new equilibrium (P2*, Q2*)?

hints.text: Set unchanged demand equal to new supply: 600 - 4P = 6P.
Solve for P2*, then substitute P2* into either 600 - 4P or 6P to verify Q2*.

options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting 600 - 4P = 6P gives 10P = 600, so P2* = $60 and Q2* = 6(60) = 360 (check: 600 - 4(60) = 360). Price falls by $12 and quantity rises by 48.
Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Shift Error): Adding the full 120-unit shift to Q1* = 312 without allowing price to fall leaves a 120-unit surplus at $72.
Diagnostic fallacy (Leftward Supply Sign Error): Subtracting 120 from supply instead of adding gives Q_s_new = -240 + 6P -> P = $84, Q = 264.
Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Shift Quantity Error): P2* = $60 is correct, but at $60 buyers only demand 600 - 4(60) = 360 units, not 312 + 120 = 432.

questions.title: Resolving Price Ambiguity Algebraically Under Simultaneous Shifts
questions.prompt_template: A market starts with Q_d = 400 - 2P and Q_s = -50 + 3P (P1* = $90, Q1* = 220). Simultaneously, demand shifts rightward by 120 units (Q_d_new = 520 - 2P) and supply shifts rightward by 70 units (Q_s_new = 20 + 3P). What is the new equilibrium (P2*, Q2*)?

hints.text: Set Q_d_new = Q_s_new: 520 - 2P = 20 + 3P.
Notice how knowing exact shift magnitudes resolves the qualitative price ambiguity: check whether P2* ends up above or below $90.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Supply Shift): Setting 520 - 2P = -50 + 3P gives P = $114 and Q = 292, forgetting to include the +70-unit rightward supply shift.

Correct. Setting 520 - 2P = 20 + 3P gives 500 = 5P, so P2* = $100 and Q2* = 520 - 2(100) = 320 (check: 20 + 3(100) = 320). Because the demand shift (+120) exceeded the supply shift (+70), equilibrium price rose by $10.
Diagnostic fallacy (Naive Cancellation & Sum Error): Assuming the opposing price effects cancel exactly at $90 and summing 220 + 120 + 70 = 410 fails to solve Q_d_new = Q_s_new.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Demand Shift): Setting 400 - 2P = 20 + 3P gives P = $76 and Q = 248, forgetting to include the +120-unit rightward demand shift.

questions.topic: Empirical Interpretation of FRED Average-Price Data
questions.title: Analytical Limits of a Single FRED Coffee Price Observation
questions.prompt_template: FRED series APU0000717311 reports a July 2026 U.S. city average price of $9.317 per pound for 100% ground-roast coffee (not seasonally adjusted). Which analytical conclusion is valid based on this single observation alone?

hints.text: Ask what information is present in one monthly price number and what information (such as quantity sold or shift drivers) is missing.
Remember the chapter's three cautions regarding FRED average-price series.

options_template.text: It proves that U.S. coffee supply shifted leftward in July 2026 while demand remained constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identification Fallacy): A single price observation cannot distinguish whether a price reflects a demand shift, a supply shift, or both—especially without quantity data.

options_template.text: It can replace the Consumer Price Index (CPI) to measure economy-wide inflation across all U.S. households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Good-as-Inflation Fallacy): One commodity's average price cannot measure economy-wide inflation; economists use aggregate indexes such as the CPI, PPI, or GDP Deflator.

options_template.text: It represents a single-product market price snapshot in a particular month; by itself it does not measure quantity sold, identify a demand or supply shift, or serve as an economy-wide inflation index.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As Chapter 3 emphasizes, APU0000717311 provides a single-product average price observation for a specific month—not a quantity measure, not causal shift identification, and not an aggregate inflation index.

options_template.text: It shows that the coffee market was in a persistent shortage during July 2026 because the price exceeded $9 per pound.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (High-Price-Equals-Shortage Fallacy): A high market price does not imply a shortage; in fact, a market-clearing equilibrium price can be high while Q_d = Q_s.

questions.topic: Diagnosing Market Shocks from Price & Quantity
questions.title: Bring It Home: Diagnosing Why Campus Latte Sales Fell
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a campus coffee shop sells fewer iced lattes this semester than last semester AND its average market-clearing price is lower than last semester. Assuming a single primary shock, which explanation from the chapter's 'Bring It Home' case best fits both facts?

hints.text: Match the observed pattern (P* fell and Q* fell) against Table 1's four single-shift signatures.
Compare a rival café opening nearby, a jump in roasted coffee-bean costs, and a menu-price hike by the shop.

options_template.text: Midterm fatigue increased student demand for iced lattes while bean costs fell.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Contradicted Quantity Direction): Simultaneous rightward demand and supply shifts must increase Q*, contradicting the observed decline in sales.

options_template.text: Roasted coffee-bean costs jumped sharply, shifting the shop's supply curve leftward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Price Signature): A leftward supply shift lowers Q* but raises P*, contradicting the observation that price fell.

options_template.text: The shop unilaterally raised its menu price from $5 to $6 while all external factors stayed constant.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Contradicted Price Direction): Raising the menu price means price rose rather than fell.

options_template.text: A new rival café opened across the street (or students switched to matcha), shifting demand for the original shop leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A leftward demand shift is the single-shift shock that pushes both equilibrium price P* and equilibrium quantity Q* downward.
