questions.topic: EV Pricing, Tax Credits, and Charging Networks
questions.title: Graphing EV Sticker Prices, Tax Credits, and Charging Complements
questions.prompt_template: In a market graph where the vertical axis measures the posted sticker price of an electric vehicle (EV), how should an economist represent (1) an automaker cutting its sticker price, (2) wider availability of fast-charging stations, and (3) a new buyer tax credit?

hints.text: Check which of the three changes alters the variable on the vertical axis (posted sticker price) versus factors outside the sticker price.
Recall Chapter 3's Real-World Application on EVs: fast charging is a complement, and a buyer tax credit lowers the buyer's effective price relative to the posted sticker price.

options_template.text: (1) moves buyers along the demand curve; (2) and (3) are both represented as rightward shifts of demand on the sticker-price graph.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A sticker-price cut moves buyers downward along demand; expanded fast-charging access raises the value of owning an EV, and a buyer tax credit lowers the effective price relative to sticker price—both shifting demand rightward at any given sticker price.

options_template.text: All three events are movements along the existing EV demand curve because all three affect what buyers care about.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis-Definition Error): Only a change in the variable plotted on the vertical axis (sticker price) moves buyers along the curve; non-sticker-price factors shift demand.

options_template.text: (1) shifts demand rightward; (2) shifts supply rightward; (3) moves buyers along demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Multiple Classification Errors): A sticker-price reduction is a movement along demand (not a shift), fast-charging access affects EV buyer demand (complement), and a buyer tax credit shifts demand on a sticker-price graph.

options_template.text: (1) and (3) both move buyers along the demand curve because a tax credit directly changes the manufacturer's posted sticker price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Effective-vs.-Posted Price Conflation): Chapter 3 explicitly notes that a buyer tax credit is not itself a change in the posted sticker price, so on a sticker-price graph it shifts demand.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting DOE Estimates of EV Lithium-Ion Battery-Pack Costs
questions.prompt_template: The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that light-duty EV lithium-ion battery-pack costs fell 90% from 2008 to 2023 (in 2023 dollars, from $1,415 to $139 per usable kWh at a scale of at least 100,000 units/year), driven by technology, chemistry, and production volume. Which economic statement accurately applies this evidence without overclaiming?

hints.text: Identify both the supply-curve implication (ceteris paribus) and the exact scope limit stated in the chapter.
Check whether the DOE estimate covers grid-scale utility storage or specifically light-duty vehicle battery packs.

options_template.text: The 90% cost drop proves that grid-scale utility battery supply shifted rightward by exactly 90% and consumer EV demand fell.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Overreach & Demand Confusion): The DOE estimate is explicitly for light-duty vehicle packs (not grid-scale storage), and lower production costs shift supply rather than reducing demand.

options_template.text: Lower unit costs can shift light-duty EV battery-pack supply rightward, ceteris paribus, but this estimate specifically applies to light-duty vehicle packs rather than grid-scale storage.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Cost declines from technology, chemistry, and scale can shift EV battery-pack supply rightward all else equal, while remaining strictly scoped to light-duty vehicle packs rather than grid-scale storage.

options_template.text: Because costs fell in 2023 dollars, EV battery-pack demand must have shifted leftward between 2008 and 2023.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shift-as-Demand-Drop Fallacy): Lower per-unit manufacturing cost shifts the supply curve rightward; it does not imply a leftward shift in consumer demand.

options_template.text: The cost drop caused a movement downward along a fixed EV battery-pack supply curve without shifting supply.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Technology-as-Movement Fallacy): Improvements in technology and chemistry lower production cost at every output level, shifting the entire supply curve rightward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Lesson from the USDA 2024/25 Brazilian Coffee Harvest Forecast
questions.prompt_template: The USDA reported severe drought and fires in Brazil from July to September 2024, yet still forecast total 2024/25 Brazilian coffee production to be 0.2% above the previous season. What methodological lesson does this case teach for real-world supply analysis?

hints.text: Compare what a textbook knee-jerk prediction ('drought always reduces total output') assumes against what the USDA aggregate forecast actually showed.
Think about why analysts must check total harvest/overall supply rather than isolating a single adverse weather headline.

options_template.text: Weather never affects agricultural supply curves, so droughts should be excluded from microeconomic models.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overcorrection Fallacy): Weather can indeed affect agricultural supply; the lesson is not that weather never matters, but that net output depends on all harvest conditions combined.

options_template.text: Droughts shift coffee demand rightward by enough to increase total coffee harvests.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Causes-Harvest Fallacy): Demand shifts do not biologically create coffee harvests during a drought; supply analysis requires evaluating overall production conditions.

options_template.text: A rigorous supply explanation must evaluate the overall harvest and net output rather than automatically assuming a single adverse input condition guarantees lower total production.
options_template.feedback: Correct. As Chapter 3 notes, while drought and fires affected conditions, total Brazilian production was still forecast 0.2% higher—showing why empirical supply analysis must account for the overall harvest rather than one isolated adverse factor.

options_template.text: Because output rose by 0.2%, the Law of Supply was violated in Brazil in 2024.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Law of Supply Misinterpretation): The Law of Supply concerns how quantity supplied responds to own price ceteris paribus; an aggregate harvest forecast reflects multiple shifting production factors.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Identifying the Dominant Shift When Both Demand and Supply Increase
questions.prompt_template: Suppose in the semiconductor market, AI server demand shifts demand rightward while new fabrication plants shift supply rightward. Over the year, analysts observe that equilibrium quantity Q* rose substantially while equilibrium price P* fell. What can be inferred about the two shifts?

hints.text: Recall which shift pushes price up and which shift pushes price down when both D and S increase.
If net price fell despite higher demand, which curve's price effect must have dominated?

options_template.text: The rightward demand shift was larger than the rightward supply shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dominant-Shift Reversal): If the rightward demand shift had dominated, equilibrium price P* would have risen rather than fallen.

options_template.text: The market failed to reach equilibrium and remained stuck in a permanent surplus.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Falling-Price-Equals-Disequilibrium Fallacy): A lower market-clearing equilibrium price is the natural result of a dominant rightward supply shift, not a failure to equilibrate.

options_template.text: The demand curve actually must have shifted leftward, because price can never fall when demand increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Shift Tunnel Vision): Price can certainly fall while demand increases if supply increases even more strongly at the same time.

options_template.text: The rightward supply shift dominated the rightward demand shift in its effect on equilibrium price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Both rightward shifts raise Q*, while demand pushes P* up and supply pushes P* down. Observing a lower P* implies the downward price pressure from the supply expansion outweighed the upward pressure from demand growth.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Inferring Dominant Shocks from Price & Quantity Data
questions.title: Using Observed Price and Quantity Movements to Separate Competing Explanations
questions.prompt_template: Over a six-month period, a city observes that the market-clearing price of artisan sourdough bread rose from $6 to $8 per loaf while the total number of loaves sold fell by 15%. Which explanation is consistent with these observations as a single-curve shift?

hints.text: Check which single curve shift raises P* and lowers Q* simultaneously.
Ask whether higher buyer demand or higher production costs produces higher prices alongside lower sales.

options_template.text: Higher flour, energy, and overtime bakery wages raised marginal costs, shifting the supply curve leftward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A leftward supply shift driven by higher input costs raises equilibrium price ($6 to $8) while reducing equilibrium quantity (-15%).

options_template.text: A viral social-media trend boosted consumer tastes for sourdough bread.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Quantity Signature): Stronger consumer tastes shift demand rightward, which raises P* AND raises Q*, contradicting the 15% drop in loaves sold.

options_template.text: A new automated baking oven lowered marginal production costs across city bakeries.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Opposite Supply Shift): Cost-reducing automation shifts supply rightward, which lowers P* and raises Q*—the exact opposite of both observations.

options_template.text: Consumer incomes fell and sourdough bread is a normal good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Price Signature): Lower income for a normal good shifts demand leftward, lowering both Q* and P* rather than raising P*.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Policy Evaluation: Per-Unit Tax vs. Production Subsidy
questions.title: Predicting Policy Trade-Offs of a Per-Unit Tax on Portable Generators
questions.prompt_template: A city considers imposing a new per-unit business tax on sellers of portable solar generators to raise municipal revenue, versus offering a per-unit production subsidy to accelerate emergency preparedness. Using the supply-and-demand model, how do the equilibrium outcomes of these two policies compare?

hints.text: Determine how each policy shifts the supply curve and trace the resulting intersection with downward-sloping demand.
Compare both the direction of market price P* paid by buyers and the equilibrium quantity Q* adopted by households.

options_template.text: The tax lowers P* because sellers must discount generators to keep buyers, while the subsidy raises P*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Price Effect): A per-unit tax reduces supply and drives market equilibrium price upward, whereas a subsidy expands supply and drives market price downward.

options_template.text: The tax shifts supply leftward (higher P*, fewer generators adopted); the subsidy shifts supply rightward (lower P*, more generators adopted).
options_template.feedback: Correct. A per-unit business tax raises sellers' marginal cost, shifting supply leftward so buyers face higher prices and buy fewer generators; a production subsidy lowers marginal cost, shifting supply rightward so prices fall and adoption expands.

options_template.text: Both policies leave Q* unchanged because household demand for emergency generators never shifts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Quantity Fallacy): Even though the demand curve does not shift, moving along a downward-sloping demand curve changes equilibrium quantity Q* whenever supply shifts.

options_template.text: The tax shifts demand leftward while leaving supply unchanged, whereas the subsidy shifts demand rightward.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Side Misattribution): Per-unit business taxes and production subsidies directly alter sellers' marginal costs and therefore shift the supply curve.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Below-Equilibrium Pricing Creates Persistent Excess Demand
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a municipal transit agency prices monthly commuter bike-locker rentals strictly below the market equilibrium price P* and prohibits price increases. According to Chapter 3's equilibrium framework, what market condition persists?

hints.text: Evaluate Q_d versus Q_s at any price below P*.
Ask what happens when upward price adjustment is blocked while Q_d exceeds Q_s.

options_template.text: A persistent surplus (excess supply), leaving many bike lockers empty at the below-equilibrium price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus-Shortage Inversion): Prices below P* generate excess demand (shortage), not excess supply (surplus).

options_template.text: Immediate market clearing, because sellers automatically expand supply rightward whenever a shortage appears.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Supply-Shift Fallacy): A shortage pressures prices upward to induce movement along supply; if price cannot rise, the supply curve does not magically shift rightward.

options_template.text: A persistent shortage (excess demand), because Q_d exceeds Q_s and prices cannot rise to clear the market.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At any price below P*, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage); if price is prevented from rising toward P*, the excess demand persists rather than clearing.

options_template.text: Zero excess demand, because buyers immediately shift their demand curve leftward when prices are low.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Disappearance Fallacy): A low own price increases quantity demanded along the curve rather than shifting demand leftward.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Critical Evaluation of Supply Curve Foundations
questions.title: Critiquing Overstatements About Diminishing Marginal Productivity
questions.prompt_template: A student writes in an essay: 'Every market supply curve in every industry must slope upward because diminishing marginal productivity is a universal technological law.' Based on Chapter 3, how should you evaluate this claim?

hints.text: Recall the exact framing in Section 3.2 regarding fixed inputs, diminishing marginal productivity, and rising marginal cost.
Check whether Chapter 3 calls diminishing marginal productivity a common short-run explanation or a universal technological law.

options_template.text: The claim is completely accurate because marginal cost always rises regardless of time horizon or technology.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uncritical Overgeneralization): Chapter 3 explicitly rejects treating diminishing marginal productivity as a universal technological law.

options_template.text: The claim is wrong because marginal cost has no connection to firms' willingness to supply output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Irrelevance Fallacy): Marginal cost is directly linked to supply—firms are willing to supply additional units when market price covers marginal cost.

options_template.text: The claim is wrong because supply curves slope upward solely due to consumer income and substitution effects.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Drivers-Applied-to-Supply): Substitution and income effects explain the downward-sloping Law of Demand, not the upward-sloping supply curve.

options_template.text: The claim is overstated: diminishing marginal productivity with fixed short-run inputs is one common reason for rising marginal cost and upward-sloping supply, not a universal technological law.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Section 3.2 explains that in many short-run settings with fixed inputs, diminishing marginal productivity can raise marginal cost—making it a common reason for upward-sloping supply, but explicitly not a universal technological law.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the Comparative Statics Derivative dP*/d(alpha)
questions.prompt_template: In Chapter 3's optional advanced section, total differentiation of Q_d(P*, alpha) - Q_s(P*) = 0 yields dP*/d(alpha) = (partial Q_d / partial alpha) / (dQ_s/dP - partial Q_d / partial P). Given partial Q_d / partial alpha > 0, dQ_s/dP > 0, and partial Q_d / partial P < 0, why is dP*/d(alpha) strictly positive and when is the price jump larger?

hints.text: Check the sign of the numerator and the sign of each term in the denominator (remember subtracting a negative number adds a positive magnitude).
Think about what happens to a positive fraction when its denominator (dQ_s/dP - partial Q_d / partial P) becomes smaller (meaning quantity responds less to price).

options_template.text: The denominator is positive because dQ_s/dP > 0 and -partial Q_d/partial P > 0, so dP*/d(alpha) > 0; the price jump is larger when buyers and sellers are less responsive to price (smaller |partial Q_d/partial P| and smaller dQ_s/dP).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Subtracting a negative demand slope makes the denominator strictly positive, proving a positive demand shock raises P*; a smaller denominator (less price responsiveness on either side) produces a larger equilibrium price increase.

options_template.text: The denominator is negative because partial Q_d / partial P < 0, which flips the sign so dP*/d(alpha) < 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Negative Sign Error): Because partial Q_d/partial P is negative, subtracting it (- partial Q_d/partial P) yields a positive term, keeping the entire denominator strictly positive.

options_template.text: The price jump is larger when dQ_s/dP is very large, because a larger denominator increases the fraction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fraction-Denominator Inversion): Making a positive denominator larger makes the quotient smaller, not larger—highly responsive supply absorbs a demand shock with a smaller price increase.

options_template.text: The formula proves that a positive demand shock raises P* while reducing equilibrium quantity Q*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Slope Sign Error): Because dQ*/d(alpha) = (dQ_s/dP)(dP*/d(alpha)) and both factors are positive, a positive demand shock raises both P* and Q*.

questions.topic: Micro vs. Macro Price Analysis in Policy Reporting
questions.title: Choosing the Right Metric for Economy-Wide Inflation vs. Single-Market Prices
questions.prompt_template: A news commentator cites a single-month FRED average retail price of ground-roast coffee ($9.317/lb in July 2026, not seasonally adjusted) as definitive proof of economy-wide inflation accelerating across the U.S. economy. How should an economist critique this reasoning?

hints.text: Recall FRED's specific caution about average-price series and the chapter's distinction between single-product prices and aggregate price indexes.
Identify both the micro-vs.-macro scope mismatch and the proper indexes economists use for economy-wide price changes over time.

options_template.text: The commentator is right because coffee is widely consumed, making its monthly average price equivalent to the GDP Deflator.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Composition Fallacy): One consumer good's price reflects product-specific supply and demand conditions, not economy-wide inflation across all domestic output.

options_template.text: FRED average-price series are best for tracking a single product's price in a particular month; measuring economy-wide price changes over time requires aggregate price indexes such as the CPI, PPI, or GDP Deflator.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Chapter 3 and FRED caution that single-product average-price series (like APU0000717311) capture one good's price in a specific month, whereas economy-wide inflation analysis requires aggregate price indexes (CPI, PPI, or GDP Deflator).

options_template.text: The commentator should only adjust the coffee price by dividing it by 12 to convert it into an accurate economy-wide inflation rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arithmetic Scaling Fallacy): Scaling a single commodity's price cannot turn a single-market observation into an economy-wide basket index.

options_template.text: The commentator is wrong only because coffee prices are always constant in equilibrium and never reflect supply or demand shocks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Price Fallacy): Single-product equilibrium prices certainly fluctuate with market shocks; the flaw is equating one product's monthly price snapshot with economy-wide inflation.
